prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- A young man carrying what turned out to be a hairbrush died Monday night in a hail of bullets fired by New York police. Khiel Coppin's brother Joel Coppin spoke briefly with reporters saying, "We want justice." Authorities were responding to a 9-1-1 call his mother made about a "family dispute with a gun," police said. In the background of the call, played at a news conference Tuesday, 18-year-old Khiel Coppin can be heard saying, "I've got a gun, I've got a gun," New York Police Department Deputy Commissioner Paul Browne told CNN. The teen put an object under his shirt and told his mother around the time she phoned 9-1-1 that he was going to say he had a gun, said New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly. The teen told her, " 'I'm prepared to die,' " Kelly told reporters. When authorities arrived at the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, the teenager had something stuffed under his shirt and several times showed a knife to police. "Shoot me, kill me," he shouted, according to Kelly. "Come get me. I have a gun. Let's do this." Coppin ignored repeated commands to stop and get on the ground. Witnesses said the teen appeared to be holding an object underneath his shirt and pointed it at the officers. Coppin continued to approach officers, as they ordered him to stop, said Kelly. Twenty shots were fired; Coppin was struck eight times, Kelly said. "This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel's family, no doubt about it," said Kelly. But the commissioner stressed that officers reasonably believed they were about to receive fire. Kelly said the teen's mother reported he had not taken his anti-depressant and anti-psychotic medication. Police have not recovered a gun and do not believe that Coppin was armed, Kelly said. A reporter asked Kelly if it's possible the young man was goading police to shoot him, a phenomenon known commonly in law enforcement circles as suicide-by-cop. "That's certainly a possibility," said Kelly. "The boy didn't have no gun, he had a brush on him," said Andre Wildman, a neighbor who told CNN that he saw the shooting.  Listen to mother's 911 call » . Another neighbor, Wayne Holder, said police should be required to see a weapon before opening fire on a suspect. "At least see a gun before you start to discharge it," Holder said. Police "don't even have to see it, [if] they think you got one, you're going to get shot." Coppin was taken to a hospital where he was declared dead. An autopsy is scheduled for Tuesday, the medical examiner's office said. The Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network is expected to hold a news conference on Tuesday about the shooting. Police said they were investigating whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had tried to have him hospitalized earlier Monday. The shooting came a year after unarmed groom Sean Bell, 23, was killed hours before his wedding in a shooting involving New York police. In 1999, unarmed African immigrant Amadou Diallo, 22, died when police in the Bronx shot him 19 times. Bystander Dyshawn Gibson described Monday's shooting to CNN affiliate WABC-TV. "He dropped the brush," Gibson said. "He put his hands up. Police just started firing." Coppin was seen pacing around the apartment prior to the shooting, according to an initial police statement issued Monday night. "He began screaming from the window at his mother and the police," the police statement said. "At some point, the male climbed out of the window and began crossing the sidewalk toward the police." That's when police began firing, a police spokesman said. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Jennifer Rizzo, Janine Brady and Alina Cho contributed to this report. Copyright 2007 CNN. “This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel’s family, no doubt about it,” Kelly said. However, the commissioner stressed that the officers reasonably believed they were about to come under fire.

outputs.L2:
NEW YORK (CNN) — Khiel Coppin, a young man who was carrying an object later identified as a hairbrush, was killed Monday evening after New York City police officers fired 20 rounds at him.

Speaking briefly to the media, his brother, Joel Coppin, called for justice.

Police said they went to the scene after Coppin’s mother called 911 to report a domestic conflict involving a gun. During a recording of the call played at a Tuesday news conference, the 18-year-old can be heard repeatedly claiming that he had a firearm, NYPD Deputy Commissioner Paul Browne told CNN.

Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly said Coppin placed an item beneath his shirt and, around the time of the emergency call, told his mother that he intended to claim he was armed. According to Kelly, Coppin also said he was ready to die.

When officers reached the family’s Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, Coppin had something concealed under his shirt and displayed a knife to police several times. Kelly said the teenager challenged officers to shoot and kill him, urged them to come for him, claimed to have a gun and said they should proceed.

Despite repeated police instructions to stop and lie on the ground, Coppin continued moving toward the officers. Witnesses said he appeared to aim an object hidden beneath his shirt at them. Officers fired 20 shots, eight of which struck Coppin, Kelly said.

Kelly described the death as unquestionably devastating for Coppin’s family but emphasized that the officers had reasonable grounds to believe they were about to be fired upon.

According to the commissioner, Coppin’s mother said her son had not taken his antidepressant or antipsychotic medicine. Investigators found no firearm and did not believe he had been armed.

Asked whether Coppin might have been deliberately provoking officers into killing him—an occurrence commonly called “suicide by cop” in law-enforcement circles—Kelly said that explanation was possible.

Andre Wildman, a neighbor who told CNN he witnessed the incident, said Coppin had no gun and was carrying only a brush. Audio of the mother’s 911 call was also made available.

Another resident, Wayne Holder, argued that officers should have to visually confirm that a suspect has a weapon before firing. He said police should at least see a gun before discharging their own weapons, adding that merely believing someone is armed can result in that person being shot.

Coppin was transported to a hospital and pronounced dead there. The medical examiner’s office said an autopsy was planned for Tuesday.

The National Action Network, led by the Rev. Al Sharpton, was expected to conduct a Tuesday news conference concerning the shooting.

Authorities said they were looking into whether Coppin had previously experienced mental illness and whether his mother had attempted to have him admitted to a hospital earlier on Monday.

The incident occurred one year after Sean Bell, an unarmed 23-year-old groom, was fatally shot by New York police only hours before his wedding. It also followed the 1999 death of Amadou Diallo, an unarmed 22-year-old African immigrant who was hit 19 times by police gunfire in the Bronx.

Dyshawn Gibson, who witnessed Monday’s shooting, gave a different account to CNN affiliate WABC-TV. Gibson said Coppin dropped the brush and raised his hands before officers began shooting.

An initial police account released Monday night stated that Coppin had been walking back and forth inside the apartment before the gunfire. Police said he then shouted from a window at both his mother and officers. At some stage, according to that statement, he climbed through the window and moved across the sidewalk in the direction of police. A department spokesman said officers opened fire at that point.

The original report included an option to send the article by email.

CNN journalists Jennifer Rizzo, Janine Brady and Alina Cho contributed to the story, as did The Associated Press.

Copyright 2007 CNN. All rights reserved. The material may not be republished, aired, rewritten or distributed.

New York City police officers responding to a 911 call about a family dispute fatally shot 18-year-old Khiel Coppin after a confrontation in which they believed he was armed. According to police, Coppin’s mother called for help after an argument and reported that her son had a knife. When officers arrived, Coppin allegedly claimed that he also had a gun, displayed the knife, and refused repeated commands to show his hands.

Police said Coppin then moved toward the officers while holding an object beneath his shirt. When he pulled out the object and pointed it in their direction, several officers opened fire, believing that he was about to shoot. Coppin was hit eight times and later died. Investigators subsequently determined that the object in his hand was a hairbrush, not a firearm.

The discovery that Coppin had been unarmed prompted questions about whether the shooting could have been avoided and whether officers had used excessive force. Police officials, however, maintained that the officers had only seconds to react and reasonably believed they faced an immediate threat of gunfire, given Coppin’s statements, his possession of a knife, and his movements during the encounter.

Authorities also raised the possibility that Coppin had deliberately provoked the officers into shooting him, a scenario sometimes described as “suicide by cop.” The case nevertheless intensified public scrutiny of police tactics, particularly in encounters involving emotionally distressed people and objects mistakenly perceived as weapons.
